queries.title: Premium products above Rs 10,000
queries.description: SELECT 1 (DML: SELECT + WHERE + ORDER BY) Business question: which products cost more than Rs 10,000, most expensive first, and how much discount do they show against MRP?
queries.sql:
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       brand,
       price,
       mrp,
       ROUND((mrp - price) / mrp * 100, 1) AS pct_off
FROM   products
WHERE  price > 10000
ORDER  BY price DESC

queries.title: Customers per city
queries.description: SELECT 2 (DML: SELECT + GROUP BY + ORDER BY) Business question: in which cities do our customers live? (Each customer has exactly one default address.)
queries.sql:
SELECT city,
       state,
       COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM   customer_addresses
WHERE  is_default = TRUE
GROUP  BY city, state
ORDER  BY customers DESC, city

queries.title: Categories with 3 or more products
queries.description: SELECT 3 (DML: SELECT + GROUP BY + HAVING) Business question: which categories have 3 or more products, and what is their average price?
queries.sql:
SELECT category_id,
       COUNT(*)             AS products,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price,
       MIN(price)           AS cheapest,
       MAX(price)           AS costliest
FROM   products
GROUP  BY category_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER  BY products DESC, category_id

queries.title: Orders by status
queries.description: SELECT 4 (DML: SELECT + GROUP BY) Business question: how many orders are in each status?
queries.sql:
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM   orders
GROUP  BY status
ORDER  BY orders DESC

queries.title: Payment attempts by method and status (more than 5)
queries.description: SELECT 5 (DML: SELECT + GROUP BY on two columns + HAVING + ORDER BY) Business question: how do payment attempts split by method and status? Show only combinations that happened more than 5 times.
queries.sql:
SELECT method,
       status,
       COUNT(*)    AS attempts,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM   payments
GROUP  BY method, status
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER  BY method, attempts DESC

queries.title: Stock below reorder level
queries.description: SELECT 6 (DML: SELECT + WHERE comparing two columns + ORDER BY) Business question: which stock rows are still below their reorder level after the Bhiwandi restock?
queries.sql:
SELECT product_id,
       warehouse_id,
       quantity,
       reorder_level
FROM   inventory
WHERE  quantity < reorder_level
ORDER  BY quantity, product_id

queries.title: Diwali-week orders by customers named A...
queries.description: SELECT 7 (DML: SELECT + WHERE with BETWEEN and LIKE) Business question: which orders were placed during the Diwali sale week (2026-10-25 to 2026-11-01) by customers whose name starts with 'A'?
queries.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.order_date,
       c.full_name,

FROM   orders o, customers c

queries.title: J1 INNER JOIN - products with their category
queries.description: J1. INNER JOIN (2 tables) Business question: what is each product's category? INNER JOIN keeps only rows that have a match on both sides.
queries.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       c.category_name,
       p.price
FROM   products   p
INNER JOIN categories c ON c.category_id = p.category_id
ORDER  BY c.category_name, p.price DESC
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: J2 INNER JOIN - top 10 orders by value
queries.description: J2. INNER JOIN (3 tables) + GROUP BY Business question: which are the 10 biggest orders by value, and who placed them?
queries.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       DATE(o.order_date)                 AS order_day,
       c.full_name                        AS customer,
       COUNT(*)                           AS line_items,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)   AS order_value
FROM   orders      o
INNER JOIN customers   c  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
GROUP  BY o.order_id, o.order_date, c.full_name
ORDER  BY order_value DESC
LIMIT  10

queries.title: J3 LEFT JOIN - every customer with order count (zero included)
queries.description: J3. LEFT OUTER JOIN Business question: how many orders has EVERY customer placed, including customers who never ordered? LEFT JOIN keeps all customers; for those with no orders the order columns are NULL, and COUNT(o.order_id) counts them as 0.
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.full_name,
       c.signup_date,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_placed
FROM   customers c
LEFT OUTER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.signup_date
ORDER  BY orders_placed, c.full_name

queries.title: J4 LEFT JOIN IS NULL - products never sold
queries.description: J4. LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL (anti-join) Business question: which products have never been sold?
queries.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.sku,
       p.product_name,
       p.price
FROM   products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE  oi.product_id IS NULL
ORDER  BY p.product_id

queries.title: J5 RIGHT JOIN - every coupon with times used
queries.description: J5. RIGHT OUTER JOIN Business question: how many times was EVERY coupon used, including coupons nobody used? RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows of the table on the right (discounts).
queries.sql:
SELECT d.code,
       d.discount_type,
       d.discount_value,
       COUNT(od.order_id)                AS times_used,
       COALESCE(SUM(od.amount_saved), 0) AS total_saved
FROM   order_discounts od
RIGHT OUTER JOIN discounts d ON d.discount_id = od.discount_id
GROUP  BY d.discount_id, d.code, d.discount_type, d.discount_value
ORDER  BY times_used DESC

queries.title: J6 FULL OUTER JOIN (emulated) - customer cities vs warehouse cities
queries.description: J6. FULL OUTER JOIN (emulated) Business question: which customer cities have no warehouse, and which warehouse cities have no customers? (Where should the next warehouse go?) MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN keyword. Standard emulation: LEFT JOIN  (all left rows + matches) UNION      (combine and REMOVE the duplicate matched rows) RIGHT JOIN (all right rows + matches) UNION ALL would show every matched city twice, so UNION is used.
queries.sql:
SELECT cc.city          AS customer_city,
       cc.customers,
       w.city           AS warehouse_city,
       w.warehouse_name
FROM   (SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
        FROM   customer_addresses
        WHERE  is_default = TRUE
        GROUP  BY city) AS cc
LEFT JOIN warehouses w ON w.city = cc.city
UNION
SELECT cc.city,
       cc.customers,
       w.city,
       w.warehouse_name
FROM   (SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers
        FROM   customer_addresses
        WHERE  is_default = TRUE
        GROUP  BY city) AS cc
RIGHT JOIN warehouses w ON w.city = cc.city
ORDER  BY warehouse_city IS NULL, customer_city

queries.title: J7 SELF JOIN - category and its parent
queries.description: J7. SELF JOIN (categories) Business question: what is the parent of each category? The same table is used twice with two aliases: child and parent. LEFT JOIN so that top-level categories (no parent) are kept.
queries.sql:
SELECT child.category_id,
       child.category_name,
       parent.category_name AS parent_category
FROM   categories child
LEFT JOIN categories parent ON parent.category_id = child.parent_category_id
ORDER  BY child.category_id

queries.title: J8 SELF JOIN - full 3-level category path
queries.description: J8. SELF JOIN, three levels Business question: show the full path of every 3rd-level category, e.g. Electronics > Mobiles > Smartphones. (A recursive CTE in 12_window_functions_ctes.sql does this for any depth; a self join needs one join per level.)
queries.sql:
SELECT top_level.category_name AS level_1,
       mid_level.category_name AS level_2,
       leaf.category_name      AS level_3,
       CONCAT(top_level.category_name, ' > ', mid_level.category_name,
              ' > ', leaf.category_name) AS full_path
FROM   categories leaf
JOIN   categories mid_level ON mid_level.category_id = leaf.parent_category_id
JOIN   categories top_level ON top_level.category_id = mid_level.parent_category_id
ORDER  BY full_path

queries.title: J9 SELF JOIN - who referred whom
queries.description: J9. SELF JOIN (customer referrals) Business question: which customer referred whom?
queries.sql:
SELECT referrer.customer_id AS referrer_id,
       referrer.full_name   AS referred_by,
       newbie.customer_id   AS customer_id,
       newbie.full_name     AS customer,
       newbie.signup_date
FROM   customers newbie
JOIN   customers referrer ON referrer.customer_id = newbie.referred_by
ORDER  BY referrer.full_name, newbie.signup_date

queries.title: J9b SELF JOIN + GROUP BY - top referrers
queries.description: Business question: which customers brought in the most new customers?
queries.sql:
SELECT referrer.full_name AS referrer,
       COUNT(*)           AS customers_referred
FROM   customers newbie
JOIN   customers referrer ON referrer.customer_id = newbie.referred_by
GROUP  BY referrer.customer_id, referrer.full_name
ORDER  BY customers_referred DESC, referrer

queries.title: J10 8-table JOIN - last 7 days, full order and payment picture
queries.description: J10. 8-table join: order and payment analysis Business question: for every order of the last 7 days, show the full picture: customer, city, items, value, coupon, payment and delivery. INNER JOIN where a row must exist (customer, items); LEFT JOIN where it may not (address, coupon, payment, delivery). Only the non-failed payment is joined, so failed retries do not double the item rows.
queries.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       DATE(o.order_date)                AS order_day,
       c.full_name                       AS customer,
       a.city,
       COUNT(oi.product_id)              AS items,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)  AS items_value,
       d.code                            AS coupon,
       pay.method                        AS pay_method,
       pay.status                        AS pay_status,
       dl.status                         AS delivery_status,
       o.status                          AS order_status
FROM   orders o
JOIN   customers          c   ON c.customer_id   = o.customer_id
JOIN   order_items        oi  ON oi.order_id     = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN customer_addresses a   ON a.address_id    = o.shipping_address_id
LEFT JOIN order_discounts    od  ON od.order_id     = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN discounts          d   ON d.discount_id   = od.discount_id
LEFT JOIN payments           pay ON pay.order_id    = o.order_id
                                AND pay.status     <> 'FAILED'
LEFT JOIN deliveries         dl  ON dl.order_id     = o.order_id
WHERE  o.order_date >= '2026-11-13'
GROUP  BY o.order_id, o.order_date, c.full_name, a.city, d.code,
          pay.method, pay.status, dl.status, o.status
ORDER  BY o.order_date

queries.title: J11 5-table JOIN - revenue by category and payment method
queries.description: J11. 5-table join + GROUP BY: payment analysis Business question: how much revenue did each top-level category earn through each payment method? (Successful payments on orders that were not cancelled; gross item value before coupons.)
queries.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(top_cat.category_name, mid_cat.category_name) AS category,
       pay.method,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)       AS orders,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS gross_revenue
FROM   order_items oi
JOIN   orders      o       ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
JOIN   payments    pay     ON pay.order_id   = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
JOIN   products    p       ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
JOIN   categories  leaf    ON leaf.category_id = p.category_id
JOIN   categories  mid_cat ON mid_cat.category_id = leaf.parent_category_id




LEFT JOIN categories top_cat ON top_cat.category_id = mid_cat.parent_category_id
WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY COALESCE(top_cat.category_name, mid_cat.category_name), pay.method
ORDER  BY category, gross_revenue DESC

queries.title: J12 CROSS JOIN - product/warehouse pairs with no stock row
queries.description: J12. CROSS JOIN + LEFT JOIN Business question: which products are NOT stocked at all in some warehouse? CROSS JOIN builds every product x warehouse pair (40 x 3 = 120); the LEFT JOIN then finds the pairs with no inventory row.
queries.sql:
SELECT p.sku,
       p.product_name,
       w.warehouse_name
FROM   products p
CROSS JOIN warehouses w
LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.product_id   = p.product_id
                     AND i.warehouse_id = w.warehouse_id
WHERE  i.product_id IS NULL
ORDER  BY w.warehouse_id, p.sku
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: S1 IN - customers who bought an Apple product
queries.description: S1. Nested subquery with IN Business question: which customers have bought at least one Apple product?
queries.sql:
SELECT customer_id, full_name
FROM   customers
WHERE  customer_id IN (
         SELECT o.customer_id
         FROM   orders o
         WHERE  o.order_id IN (
                  SELECT oi.order_id
                  FROM   order_items oi
                  WHERE  oi.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM products WHERE brand = 'Apple')))
ORDER  BY full_name

queries.title: S2 NOT IN - active products with no sale in November
queries.description: S2. Nested subquery with NOT IN Business question: which active products were not sold even once in November 2026? Caution: NOT IN returns NO rows if the subquery contains a NULL. order_items.product_id is NOT NULL, so it is safe here; in general NOT EXISTS (S12) is the safer choice.
queries.sql:
SELECT product_id, sku, product_name
FROM   products
WHERE  is_active = TRUE
  AND  product_id NOT IN (
         SELECT oi.product_id
         FROM   order_items oi
         WHERE  oi.order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders
                                WHERE  order_date >= '2026-11-01'))
ORDER  BY product_id

queries.title: S3 scalar subquery - products above the overall average price
queries.description: S3. Scalar subquery in WHERE Business question: which products cost more than the average product? A scalar subquery returns exactly one value (one row, one column).
queries.sql:
SELECT product_id, product_name, price
FROM   products
WHERE  price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)
ORDER  BY price DESC

queries.title: S4 scalar subquery in SELECT - price vs catalogue average
queries.description: S4. Scalar subquery in SELECT Business question: how far is each product's price from the catalogue average?
queries.sql:
SELECT product_name,
       price,
       ROUND((SELECT AVG(price) FROM products), 2)         AS catalogue_avg,
       ROUND(price - (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products), 2) AS diff_from_avg
FROM   products
ORDER  BY diff_from_avg DESC
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: S5 multi-level nesting - customers of the best-selling category
queries.description: S5. Multi-level nesting (4 levels deep) Business question: which customers bought something from our best-selling category (by units sold)? Read from the inside out: level 4: best category  -> level 3: its products level 2: orders containing them -> level 1: their customers (MySQL does not allow LIMIT directly inside IN (...), so the "top 1" is wrapped in a derived table.)
queries.sql:
SELECT customer_id, full_name
FROM   customers
WHERE  customer_id IN (
         SELECT customer_id FROM orders
         WHERE  order_id IN (
                  SELECT order_id FROM order_items
                  WHERE  product_id IN (
                           SELECT product_id FROM products
                           WHERE  category_id = (
                                    SELECT category_id
                                    FROM  (SELECT p.category_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units
                                           FROM   order_items oi
                                           JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
                                           GROUP  BY p.category_id
                                           ORDER  BY units DESC
                                           LIMIT  1) AS best))))
ORDER  BY full_name

queries.title: S6a ALL - products costlier than every book
queries.description: S6. ALL and ANY Business question (a): which products cost more than EVERY book? > ALL (list)  means  greater than the maximum of the list. Business question (b): which products are cheaper than AT LEAST ONE book? < ANY (list)  means  less than the maximum of the list.
queries.sql:
SELECT product_name, price
FROM   products
WHERE  price > ALL (SELECT p.price
                    FROM   products p
                    WHERE  p.category_id IN (SELECT category_id FROM categories
                                             WHERE  parent_category_id =
                                                    (SELECT category_id FROM categories
                                                     WHERE  category_name = 'Books')))
ORDER  BY price
LIMIT  10
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: S6b ANY - non-book products cheaper than at least one book
queries.description: (22, 23 = Fiction and Non-Fiction, the two Books sub-categories) Subqueries (ANY) | Business question: which non-book products cost less than at least one book?
queries.sql:
SELECT product_name, price
FROM   products
WHERE  category_id NOT IN (22, 23)
  AND  price < ANY (SELECT price FROM products WHERE category_id IN (22, 23))
ORDER  BY price

queries.title: S7 correlated - products above their category average
queries.description: S7. Correlated subquery in WHERE Business question: which products are priced above THEIR OWN category's average? p2.category_id = p.category_id links the inner query to the outer row, so the category average is recalculated for every product.
queries.sql:
SELECT p.product_name,
       p.category_id,
       p.price,
       (SELECT ROUND(AVG(p2.price), 2)
        FROM   products p2
        WHERE  p2.category_id = p.category_id) AS category_avg
FROM   products p
WHERE  p.price > (SELECT AVG(p2.price)
                  FROM   products p2
                  WHERE  p2.category_id = p.category_id)
ORDER  BY p.category_id, p.price DESC
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: S8 correlated - each customer's latest order
queries.description: S8. Correlated subquery: latest row per group Business question: what is each customer's most recent order?
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.full_name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_date,
       o.status
FROM   orders o
JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE  o.order_date = (SELECT MAX(o2.order_date)
                       FROM   orders o2
                       WHERE  o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
ORDER  BY o.order_date DESC

queries.title: S9 correlated in SELECT - orders and spend per customer (top 15)
queries.description: S9. Correlated subqueries in SELECT Business question: for each customer, how many orders have they placed and how much have they actually paid (successful payments on orders that were not cancelled)? Top 15 by spend.
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.full_name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM   orders o
        WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS orders_placed,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0)
        FROM   payments p
        JOIN   orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
        WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
          AND  p.status = 'SUCCESS'
          AND  o.status <> 'CANCELLED') AS total_spend
FROM   customers c
ORDER  BY total_spend DESC, c.customer_id
LIMIT  15

queries.title: S10 correlated - orders above the customer's own average
queries.description: S10. Correlated subquery comparing a row with its own group Business question: which orders were bigger than that customer's OWN average order value? (A sign of an unusually large purchase.) customer's average = all their item value / number of their orders
queries.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.customer_id,
       (SELECT SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
        FROM   order_items oi
        WHERE  oi.order_id = o.order_id) AS order_value,
       ROUND((SELECT SUM(oi2.quantity * oi2.unit_price)
              FROM   order_items oi2
              JOIN   orders o2 ON o2.order_id = oi2.order_id
              WHERE  o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
           / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o3 WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id), 2)
                                         AS customer_avg
FROM   orders o
WHERE  (SELECT SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
        FROM   order_items oi
        WHERE  oi.order_id = o.order_id)
     > (SELECT SUM(oi2.quantity * oi2.unit_price)
        FROM   order_items oi2
        JOIN   orders o2 ON o2.order_id = oi2.order_id
        WHERE  o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
     / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o3 WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id)
ORDER  BY o.customer_id, o.order_id

queries.title: S11 EXISTS - customers with at least one failed payment
queries.description: S11. EXISTS (correlated) Business question: which customers have had at least one failed payment? (Candidates for a "payment trouble?" help message.)
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name
FROM   customers c
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1
               FROM   orders o
               JOIN   payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
               WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                 AND  p.status = 'FAILED')
ORDER  BY c.full_name

queries.title: S12 NOT EXISTS - customers who never ordered
queries.description: S12. NOT EXISTS (correlated) Business question: which customers signed up but never placed an order? (Target them with the WELCOME100 coupon.)
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.signup_date
FROM   customers c
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                   FROM   orders o
                   WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER  BY c.signup_date

queries.title: S13 derived tables - customer segments by average order value
queries.description: S13. Two levels of derived tables Business question: split customers into High / Medium / Low value by their average order value. per_order    : value of every order per_customer : average order value of every customer + segment outer query  : how many customers fall in each segment
queries.sql:
SELECT segment,
       COUNT(*)                         AS customers,
       ROUND(AVG(avg_order_value), 2)   AS avg_order_value
FROM  (SELECT customer_id,
              AVG(order_value) AS avg_order_value,
              CASE
                  WHEN AVG(order_value) >= 20000 THEN 'High'
                  WHEN AVG(order_value) >= 5000  THEN 'Medium'
                  ELSE 'Low'
              END AS segment
       FROM  (SELECT o.customer_id,
                     o.order_id,
                     SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS order_value
              FROM   orders o
              JOIN   order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
              GROUP  BY o.customer_id, o.order_id) AS per_order
       GROUP  BY customer_id) AS per_customer
GROUP  BY segment
ORDER  BY avg_order_value DESC

queries.title: S14 derived table - months above the average monthly revenue
queries.description: S14. Derived table + scalar subquery Business question: which months earned more than the average month? (Revenue = successful payments on orders that were not cancelled.) The same derived table is written twice here; a CTE (WITH ...) in 12_window_functions_ctes.sql removes that repetition.
queries.sql:
SELECT m.month,
       m.revenue
FROM  (SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
              SUM(p.amount)                      AS revenue
       FROM   orders o
       JOIN   payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
       WHERE  p.status = 'SUCCESS' AND o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
       GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')) AS m
WHERE  m.revenue > (SELECT AVG(m2.revenue)
                    FROM  (SELECT SUM(p.amount) AS revenue
                           FROM   orders o
                           JOIN   payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
                           WHERE  p.status = 'SUCCESS' AND o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
                           GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')) AS m2)
ORDER  BY m.month

queries.title: U1 UNION - customers who paid by UPI or card
queries.description: U1. UNION Business question: which customers have paid successfully by UPI OR by card? Each customer appears once.
queries.sql:
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'UPI'  AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
UNION
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'CARD' AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
ORDER  BY customer_id

queries.title: U2 UNION ALL - same list, duplicates kept
queries.description: U2. UNION ALL Business question: the same list, but WITHOUT removing duplicates. DISTINCT inside each half gives one row per customer per method, so a customer who used both methods appears exactly twice.
queries.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id, 'UPI' AS method
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'UPI'  AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
UNION ALL
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id, 'CARD'
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'CARD' AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
ORDER  BY customer_id, method

queries.title: U3 UNION vs UNION ALL - row counts
queries.description: U3. UNION vs UNION ALL, side by side Business question: how many rows does each version return, and why?
queries.sql:
SELECT 'UNION (duplicates removed)' AS version, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM  (SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
       WHERE  p.method = 'UPI'  AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
       UNION
       SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
       WHERE  p.method = 'CARD' AND p.status = 'SUCCESS') AS u
UNION ALL
SELECT 'UNION ALL (duplicates kept)', COUNT(*)
FROM  (SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
       WHERE  p.method = 'UPI'  AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
       UNION ALL
       SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
       WHERE  p.method = 'CARD' AND p.status = 'SUCCESS') AS ua

queries.title: U4 UNION - every city with a customer or a warehouse
queries.description: U4. UNION across two different tables Business question: in which cities do we have customers OR a warehouse? (Our full "presence" map.) A city that has both appears only once.
queries.sql:
SELECT city FROM customer_addresses WHERE is_default = TRUE
UNION
SELECT city FROM warehouses
ORDER  BY city

queries.title: I1 INTERSECT - customers who paid by both UPI and card
queries.description: I1. INTERSECT Business question: which customers have paid successfully by BOTH UPI AND card? (They are comfortable with digital payments: good targets for a card-linked UPI cashback offer.)
queries.sql:
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'UPI'  AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
INTERSECT
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'CARD' AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
ORDER  BY customer_id

queries.title: I1b INTERSECT equivalent with IN - same customers as I1
queries.description: I1b. INTERSECT equivalent for MySQL older than 8.0.31: IN Business question: the same as I1.
queries.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE  p.method = 'UPI' AND p.status = 'SUCCESS'
  AND  o.customer_id IN (SELECT o2.customer_id
                         FROM   orders o2 JOIN payments p2 ON p2.order_id = o2.order_id
                         WHERE  p2.method = 'CARD' AND p2.status = 'SUCCESS')
ORDER  BY customer_id

queries.title: I2 INTERSECT - products sold in both October and November
queries.description: I2. INTERSECT Business question: which products sold in BOTH October (Diwali month) AND November? (Steady sellers, not just festive spikes.)
queries.sql:
SELECT oi.product_id
FROM   order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE  o.order_date >= '2026-10-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-11-01'
INTERSECT
SELECT oi.product_id
FROM   order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE  o.order_date >= '2026-11-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-12-01'
ORDER  BY product_id

queries.title: E1 EXCEPT - customers who ordered but never used a coupon
queries.description: E1. EXCEPT (this is what Oracle writes as MINUS) Business question: which customers placed orders but NEVER used a coupon? (Send them a first-coupon offer.) Oracle:  SELECT customer_id FROM orders MINUS SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN order_discounts od ...
queries.sql:
SELECT customer_id
FROM   orders
EXCEPT
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o JOIN order_discounts od ON od.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER  BY customer_id

queries.title: E1b MINUS equivalent with NOT EXISTS - same customers as E1
queries.description: E1b. MINUS equivalent no. 1: NOT EXISTS Business question: the same as E1 (works on every MySQL version).
queries.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                   FROM   orders o2 JOIN order_discounts od ON od.order_id = o2.order_id
                   WHERE  o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
ORDER  BY customer_id

queries.title: E1c MINUS equivalent with LEFT JOIN IS NULL - same customers as E1
queries.description: E1c. MINUS equivalent no. 2: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL Business question: the same as E1.
queries.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id
FROM   orders o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT o2.customer_id
           FROM   orders o2 JOIN order_discounts od ON od.order_id = o2.order_id) AS used
       ON used.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE  used.customer_id IS NULL
ORDER  BY customer_id

queries.title: E2 EXCEPT - catalogue minus sold products
queries.description: E2. EXCEPT Business question: which catalogue products have never been sold? (All products MINUS the products that appear in order_items.)
queries.sql:
SELECT product_id, sku FROM products
EXCEPT
SELECT p.product_id, p.sku
FROM   products p JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER  BY product_id

queries.title: A1 Repeat customers (more than 1 order)
queries.description: A1. Repeat customers (JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING) Business question: which customers have ordered more than once, and how loyal and valuable are they?
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.full_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)          AS orders_placed,
       DATE(MIN(o.order_date))             AS first_order,
       DATE(MAX(o.order_date))             AS last_order,
       COALESCE(SUM(pay.amount), 0)        AS net_spend
FROM   customers c
JOIN   orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN payments pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id
                      AND pay.status   = 'SUCCESS'
                      AND o.status    <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.full_name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) > 1
ORDER  BY orders_placed DESC, net_spend DESC

queries.title: A2 Repeat purchase rate
queries.description: A2. Repeat purchase rate (derived table) Business question: out of all customers who ordered, what percentage came back for another order?
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                  AS ordering_customers,
       SUM(order_count > 1)                      AS repeat_customers,
       SUM(order_count = 1)                      AS one_time_customers,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(order_count > 1) / COUNT(*), 1) AS repeat_rate_pct
FROM  (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
       FROM   orders
       GROUP  BY customer_id) AS per_customer

queries.title: A3 Top 10 customers by net spend
queries.description: A3. Top customers by net spend (4-table join) Business question: who are our 10 most valuable customers?
queries.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.full_name,
       a.city,
       COUNT(*)                  AS paid_orders,
       SUM(pay.amount)           AS net_spend,
       ROUND(AVG(pay.amount), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM   customers c
JOIN   orders   o   ON o.customer_id  = c.customer_id
JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id   = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
LEFT JOIN customer_addresses a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.is_default = TRUE
WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY c.customer_id, c.full_name, a.city
ORDER  BY net_spend DESC
LIMIT  10

queries.title: A4 Referred vs direct customers
queries.description: A4. Referral impact (correlated subqueries inside a derived table) Business question: do referred customers order more and spend more than customers who came directly?
queries.sql:
SELECT source,
       COUNT(*)                 AS customers,
       ROUND(AVG(orders), 2)    AS avg_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(spend), 2)     AS avg_net_spend,
       SUM(orders = 0)          AS never_ordered
FROM  (SELECT c.customer_id,
              IF(c.referred_by IS NULL, 'Direct', 'Referred') AS source,
              (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS orders,
              (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(p.amount), 0)
               FROM   payments p JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
               WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                 AND  p.status = 'SUCCESS' AND o.status <> 'CANCELLED') AS spend
       FROM   customers c) AS per_customer
GROUP  BY source
ORDER  BY source

queries.title: B1 Best-selling products by quantity (top 10)
queries.description: B1. Best-selling products by QUANTITY Business question: which 10 products sell the most units?
queries.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       cat.category_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity)                  AS units_sold,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)       AS orders,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)  AS gross_value
FROM   order_items oi
JOIN   orders     o   ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
JOIN   products   p   ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
JOIN   categories cat ON cat.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY p.product_id, p.product_name, cat.category_name
ORDER  BY units_sold DESC, gross_value DESC
LIMIT  10

queries.title: B2 Best-selling products by revenue (top 10)
queries.description: B2. Best-selling products by REVENUE Business question: which 10 products bring in the most money? (Different from B1: a cable sells many units cheaply, a phone sells fewer units but earns far more.)
queries.sql:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       cat.category_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity)                  AS units_sold,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)  AS gross_value,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
             / (SELECT SUM(oi2.quantity * oi2.unit_price)
                FROM   order_items oi2 JOIN orders o2 ON o2.order_id = oi2.order_id
                WHERE  o2.status <> 'CANCELLED'), 2) AS share_pct
FROM   order_items oi
JOIN   orders     o   ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
JOIN   products   p   ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
JOIN   categories cat ON cat.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY p.product_id, p.product_name, cat.category_name
ORDER  BY gross_value DESC
LIMIT  10

queries.title: B3 Best-selling product per category
queries.description: B3. Best-selling product in EACH category (without window functions) Business question: what is the number-one product (by units) in every category? Method: product totals JOIN category maximum ON units = maximum. If two products tie for the top spot, both are shown (that is the correct answer; ROW_NUMBER() in file 12 shows how to force one).
queries.sql:
SELECT cat.category_name,
       s.product_name,
       s.units_sold
FROM  (SELECT p.category_id, p.product_id, p.product_name,
              SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold
       FROM   order_items oi
       JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
       JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
       WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
       GROUP  BY p.category_id, p.product_id, p.product_name) AS s
JOIN  (SELECT category_id, MAX(units_sold) AS max_units
       FROM  (SELECT p.category_id, p.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold
              FROM   order_items oi
              JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
              JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
              WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
              GROUP  BY p.category_id, p.product_id) AS t
       GROUP  BY category_id) AS m
       ON m.category_id = s.category_id AND m.max_units = s.units_sold
JOIN   categories cat ON cat.category_id = s.category_id
ORDER  BY s.units_sold DESC, cat.category_name

queries.title: B4 Stock of the top 10 best sellers
queries.description: B4. Stock health of the best sellers Business question: are our 10 best-selling products in stock, or do we need to reorder?
queries.sql:
SELECT top10.product_name,
       top10.units_sold,
       SUM(i.quantity)                        AS stock_all_warehouses,
       SUM(i.quantity = 0)                    AS warehouses_out_of_stock,
       SUM(i.quantity < i.reorder_level)      AS warehouses_below_reorder
FROM  (SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold
       FROM   order_items oi
       JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
       JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
       WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
       GROUP  BY p.product_id, p.product_name
       ORDER  BY units_sold DESC
       LIMIT  10) AS top10
JOIN   inventory i ON i.product_id = top10.product_id
GROUP  BY top10.product_id, top10.product_name, top10.units_sold
ORDER  BY top10.units_sold DESC

queries.title: C1 Average order value
queries.description: C1. Average order value (AOV) Business question: how much does a typical paid order bring in?
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                 AS paid_orders,
       SUM(pay.amount)          AS net_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(pay.amount), 2) AS avg_order_value,
       MIN(pay.amount)          AS smallest_order,
       MAX(pay.amount)          AS biggest_order
FROM   payments pay
JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id = pay.order_id
WHERE  pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
  AND  o.status  <> 'CANCELLED'

queries.title: C2 Revenue by payment method
queries.description: C2. Revenue by payment method (scalar subquery for the share) Business question: how do customers pay, and which method brings the most money?
queries.sql:
SELECT pay.method,
       COUNT(*)                  AS paid_orders,
       SUM(pay.amount)           AS net_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(pay.amount), 2) AS avg_order_value,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(pay.amount)
             / (SELECT SUM(p2.amount)
                FROM   payments p2 JOIN orders o2 ON o2.order_id = p2.order_id
                WHERE  p2.status = 'SUCCESS' AND o2.status <> 'CANCELLED'), 2) AS share_pct
FROM   payments pay
JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id = pay.order_id
WHERE  pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
  AND  o.status  <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY pay.method
ORDER  BY net_revenue DESC

queries.title: C3 Payment failure rate by method
queries.description: C3. Payment failure rate by method Business question: which payment method fails most often? (Talk to that payment partner.)
queries.sql:
SELECT method,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS attempts,
       SUM(status = 'SUCCESS')                    AS succeeded,
       SUM(status = 'FAILED')                     AS failed,
       SUM(status = 'PENDING')                    AS pending,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(status = 'FAILED') / COUNT(*), 1) AS failure_rate_pct
FROM   payments
GROUP  BY method
ORDER  BY failure_rate_pct DESC

queries.title: C4 Monthly revenue
queries.description: C4. Monthly revenue Business question: how did sales move month by month? (Month-over-month change with LAG() is in file 12.)
queries.sql:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       COUNT(*)                           AS paid_orders,
       SUM(pay.amount)                    AS net_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(pay.amount), 2)          AS avg_order_value
FROM   orders   o
JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER  BY month

queries.title: C5 Orders with failed or pending payments
queries.description: C5. Orders with failed or pending payments Business question: which orders had payment trouble, and where does each one stand now (recovered on retry, money still pending, or lost)?
queries.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       DATE(o.order_date)                         AS order_day,
       c.full_name                                AS customer,
       GROUP_CONCAT(CONCAT(pay.method, ':', pay.status)
                    ORDER BY pay.payment_id SEPARATOR ' -> ') AS payment_attempts,
       CASE
           WHEN SUM(pay.status = 'SUCCESS') > 0 THEN 'Recovered on retry'
           WHEN SUM(pay.status = 'PENDING') > 0 THEN 'Money pending'
           ELSE 'Failed - order cancelled'
       END                                        AS outcome,
       o.status                                   AS order_status
FROM   orders o
JOIN   customers c  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id  = o.order_id
GROUP  BY o.order_id, o.order_date, c.full_name, o.status
HAVING SUM(pay.status IN ('FAILED', 'PENDING')) > 0
ORDER  BY outcome, o.order_date

queries.title: C6 Orders not yet delivered
queries.description: C6. Orders not yet delivered Business question: which live orders are still waiting for delivery, and for how many days? (Oldest first, so support can chase them.)
queries.sql:
SELECT o.order_id,
       DATE(o.order_date)                       AS order_day,
       DATEDIFF('2026-11-20', o.order_date)     AS days_waiting,
       c.full_name                              AS customer,
       o.status                                 AS order_status,
       COALESCE(d.status, 'NOT CREATED')        AS delivery_status,
       d.courier,
       w.warehouse_name
FROM   orders o
JOIN   customers  c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN deliveries d ON d.order_id     = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN warehouses w ON w.warehouse_id = d.warehouse_id
WHERE  o.status NOT IN ('DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED')
ORDER  BY days_waiting DESC, o.order_id

queries.title: C7 Courier performance
queries.description: C7. Courier performance Business question: which courier delivers fastest, and which has the most returns?
queries.sql:
SELECT courier,
       COUNT(*)                                             AS shipments,
       SUM(status = 'DELIVERED')                            AS delivered,
       SUM(status = 'RETURNED')                             AS returned,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'DELIVERED'
                      THEN DATEDIFF(delivered_date, shipped_date) END), 2) AS avg_transit_days,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(status = 'RETURNED')
             / NULLIF(SUM(status IN ('DELIVERED', 'RETURNED')), 0), 1)   AS return_rate_pct
FROM   deliveries
GROUP  BY courier
ORDER  BY avg_transit_days

queries.title: D1 Coupon usage and impact
queries.description: D1. Coupon usage and impact Business question: how often is each coupon used, how much discount has it given away, and how big are the orders that use it?
queries.sql:
SELECT d.code,
       d.discount_type,
       d.discount_value,
       d.min_order_value,
       COUNT(od.order_id)                            AS times_used,
       COALESCE(SUM(od.amount_saved), 0)             AS total_discount_given,
       ROUND(AVG(od.amount_saved), 2)                AS avg_saving,
       ROUND(AVG((SELECT SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)
                  FROM   order_items oi
                  WHERE  oi.order_id = od.order_id)), 2) AS avg_order_gross
FROM   discounts d

queries.title: W1 ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK - products by units sold
queries.description: W1. ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK (with real ties) Business question: rank every product by units sold. On a tie (e.g. two products with 37 units): ROW_NUMBER : always 1, 2, 3, ... (ties broken by product_id), unique RANK       : ties share a rank, then a GAP  (1, 1, 3) DENSE_RANK : ties share a rank, NO gap      (1, 1, 2) The named WINDOW clause (w) avoids repeating the same OVER (...).
queries.sql:
WITH product_units AS (
    SELECT p.product_id,
           p.product_name,
           SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold
    FROM   order_items oi
    JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
    JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY p.product_id, p.product_name
)
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       units_sold,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY units_sold DESC, product_id) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER w                                      AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER w                                      AS dense_rnk
FROM   product_units
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY units_sold DESC)
ORDER  BY units_sold DESC, product_id
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: W2 RANK PARTITION BY category - product rank inside its category
queries.description: W2. RANK() with PARTITION BY category Business question: how does each product rank INSIDE its own category, by revenue and by units? PARTITION BY restarts the ranking at 1 for every category.
queries.sql:
SELECT cat.category_name,
       p.product_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity)                 AS units_sold,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS gross_value,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat.category_id
                    ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) DESC) AS revenue_rank,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat.category_id
                    ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity) DESC)                 AS units_rank
FROM   order_items oi
JOIN   orders     o   ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
JOIN   products   p   ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
JOIN   categories cat ON cat.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP  BY cat.category_id, cat.category_name, p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER  BY cat.category_name, revenue_rank
rows: U.S. Polo Assn. Crew Neck Tee

queries.title: W2b RANK = 1 - best seller per category (ties kept)
queries.description: W2b. Best-selling product per category with RANK() (compare with B3 in file 09, which needed two derived tables) Business question: the number-one product (by units) in each category, keeping ties.
queries.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT cat.category_name,
           p.product_name,
           SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat.category_id
                        ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM   order_items oi
    JOIN   orders     o   ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
    JOIN   products   p   ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
    JOIN   categories cat ON cat.category_id = p.category_id
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY cat.category_id, cat.category_name, p.product_id, p.product_name
)
SELECT category_name, product_name, units_sold
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rnk = 1
ORDER  BY units_sold DESC, category_name

queries.title: W3 ROW_NUMBER = 1 - one featured product per category
queries.description: W3. ROW_NUMBER() = 1 - exactly ONE winner per category Business question: we can feature only one product per category on the home page. On a tie in units, pick the one with more revenue.
queries.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT cat.category_name,
           p.product_name,
           SUM(oi.quantity)                 AS units_sold,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS gross_value,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY cat.category_id
                              ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity) DESC,
                                       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) DESC,
                                       p.product_id) AS rn
    FROM   order_items oi
    JOIN   orders     o   ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
    JOIN   products   p   ON p.product_id   = oi.product_id
    JOIN   categories cat ON cat.category_id = p.category_id
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY cat.category_id, cat.category_name, p.product_id, p.product_name
)
SELECT category_name, product_name, units_sold, gross_value
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rn = 1
ORDER  BY category_name

queries.title: W4 SUM OVER ORDER BY - running total of revenue
queries.description: W4. Running total with SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...) Business question: how did total revenue build up month by month, and what share of the year-to-date total had we reached each month?
queries.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
           SUM(pay.amount)                    AS revenue
    FROM   orders o
    JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                          ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                                      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
                 / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1)                                 AS pct_of_total
FROM   monthly
ORDER  BY month

queries.title: W5 LAG - month-over-month revenue change
queries.description: W5. Month-over-month change with LAG() Business question: did revenue go up or down compared with the previous month, and by how much? LAG(x) returns x from the PREVIOUS row (NULL for the first month).
queries.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
           COUNT(*)                           AS paid_orders,
           SUM(pay.amount)                    AS revenue
    FROM   orders o
    JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT month,
       paid_orders,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)             AS prev_month_revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)   AS change_amount,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
                 / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS change_pct
FROM   monthly
ORDER  BY month

queries.title: W6 AVG OVER ROWS 2 PRECEDING - 3-month moving average
queries.description: W6. Moving average with a window FRAME Business question: what is the 3-month moving average of revenue (it smooths out one-off spikes such as the Diwali sale)?
queries.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
           SUM(pay.amount)                    AS revenue
    FROM   orders o
    JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                                ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3m
FROM   monthly
ORDER  BY month

queries.title: W7 NTILE(4) - customer quartiles by lifetime value
queries.description: W7. Customer segments with NTILE(4) Business question: split paying customers into 4 equal groups by lifetime value (Q1 = top 25%). Uses the view from file 10.
queries.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       full_name,
       lifetime_value,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC, customer_id) AS quartile
FROM   vw_customer_lifetime_value
WHERE  lifetime_value > 0

queries.title: W7b NTILE(4) - size and value of each quartile
queries.description: Window functions (NTILE) + CTE | Business question: how big and how valuable is each customer quartile?
queries.sql:
WITH q AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           lifetime_value,
           NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC, customer_id) AS quartile
    FROM   vw_customer_lifetime_value
    WHERE  lifetime_value > 0
)
SELECT CONCAT('Q', quartile)              AS quartile,
       COUNT(*)                           AS customers,
       MIN(lifetime_value)                AS min_value,
       MAX(lifetime_value)                AS max_value,
       SUM(lifetime_value)                AS total_value,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(lifetime_value) / (SELECT SUM(lifetime_value) FROM q), 1) AS share_pct
FROM   q
GROUP  BY quartile
ORDER  BY quartile

queries.title: W8 LEAD - average gap between orders per repeat customer
queries.description: W8. LEAD() - days until the next order (repeat behaviour) Business question: how many days do repeat customers usually wait before ordering again? (When should the "come back" reminder go out?) LEAD(x) returns x from the NEXT row in the partition.
queries.sql:
WITH gaps AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           order_date,
           DATEDIFF(LEAD(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date),
                    order_date) AS days_to_next_order
    FROM   orders
)
SELECT g.customer_id,
       c.full_name,
       COUNT(*) + 1                       AS orders_placed,
       ROUND(AVG(g.days_to_next_order), 1) AS avg_days_between_orders,
       MIN(g.days_to_next_order)          AS shortest_gap,
       MAX(g.days_to_next_order)          AS longest_gap
FROM   gaps g
JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = g.customer_id
WHERE  g.days_to_next_order IS NOT NULL
GROUP  BY g.customer_id, c.full_name
ORDER  BY avg_days_between_orders, g.customer_id

queries.title: W9 SUM OVER () and PERCENT_RANK - product share of sales (top 15)
queries.description: W9. Share of total, PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST Business question: what share of all sales does each product make, and in which percentile does it sit? (Top 15 shown.) SUM(...) OVER () with an empty window = the grand total on every row.
queries.sql:
WITH product_value AS (
    SELECT p.product_name,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS gross_value
    FROM   order_items oi
    JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
    JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY p.product_id, p.product_name
)
SELECT product_name,
       gross_value,
       ROUND(100 * gross_value / SUM(gross_value) OVER (), 2)           AS share_pct,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(gross_value) OVER (ORDER BY gross_value DESC
                                          ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
                 / SUM(gross_value) OVER (), 1)                         AS cumulative_pct,
       

       ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY gross_value), 3)             AS pct_rank,
       ROUND(CUME_DIST()    OVER (ORDER BY gross_value), 3)             AS cumulative_dist
FROM   product_value
ORDER  BY gross_value DESC
LIMIT  15

queries.title: T1 CTE + RANK - top product of each month
queries.description: T1. Multi-step CTE: top product of every month Business question: which product sold the most units in each month? step 1 (monthly_sales): units per product per month step 2 (ranked)       : RANK() inside each month step 3 (final SELECT) : keep rank 1
queries.sql:
WITH monthly_sales AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
           p.product_name,
           SUM(oi.quantity)                   AS units_sold,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)   AS gross_value
    FROM   order_items oi
    JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
    JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m'), p.product_id, p.product_name
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT month, product_name, units_sold, gross_value,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY units_sold DESC) AS rnk
    FROM   monthly_sales
)
SELECT month, product_name, units_sold, gross_value
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rnk = 1
ORDER  BY month, product_name

queries.title: T2 CTE - cohorts by first-order month and how many came back
queries.description: T2. Multi-step CTE: customer cohorts Business question: group customers by the month of their FIRST order; how many of each group came back for another order?
queries.sql:
WITH first_orders AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_order,
           COUNT(*)        AS total_orders
    FROM   orders
    GROUP  BY customer_id
),
cohorts AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(first_order, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month,
           customer_id,
           total_orders
    FROM   first_orders
)
SELECT cohort_month,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS new_customers,
       SUM(total_orders > 1)                        AS came_back,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(total_orders > 1) / COUNT(*), 1) AS came_back_pct
FROM   cohorts
GROUP  BY cohort_month
ORDER  BY cohort_month

queries.title: T3 CTE referenced twice - months above the average monthly revenue
queries.description: T3. CTE used twice: months above the average month Business question: the same as S14 in file 07, but the monthly totals are written ONCE (in the CTE) and used twice, instead of repeating the derived table.
queries.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
           SUM(pay.amount)                    AS revenue
    FROM   orders o
    JOIN   payments pay ON pay.order_id = o.order_id AND pay.status = 'SUCCESS'
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m')
)
SELECT month, revenue
FROM   monthly
WHERE  revenue > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM monthly)
ORDER  BY month

queries.title: R1 WITH RECURSIVE - full category tree
queries.description: R1. Recursive CTE: the full category tree Business question: show every category with its level and full path, for ANY depth (the self join in J8 needed one join per level).
queries.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE category_tree AS (
    

    SELECT category_id,
           category_name,
           parent_category_id,
           1                               AS level,
           CAST(category_name AS CHAR(255)) AS path
    FROM   categories
    WHERE  parent_category_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    

    SELECT c.category_id,
           c.category_name,
           c.parent_category_id,
           t.level + 1,
           CONCAT(t.path, ' > ', c.category_name)
    FROM   categories c
    JOIN   category_tree t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id
    WHERE  t.level < 10
)
SELECT category_id,
       CONCAT(REPEAT('    ', level - 1), category_name) AS indented_name,
       level,
       path
FROM   category_tree
ORDER  BY path

queries.title: R2 WITH RECURSIVE - sales rolled up to each top-level category
queries.description: R2. Recursive CTE + roll-up Business question: how much has each TOP-LEVEL category sold in total, counting all of its sub-categories at every depth? Each row carries its root (top-level) category down the tree.
queries.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE branch AS (
    SELECT category_id   AS root_id,
           category_name AS root_name,
           category_id,
           1             AS level
    FROM   categories
    WHERE  parent_category_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b.root_id, b.root_name, c.category_id, b.level + 1
    FROM   categories c
    JOIN   branch b ON c.parent_category_id = b.category_id
    WHERE  b.level < 10
),
category_sales AS (
    SELECT p.category_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id)     AS products_sold,
           SUM(oi.quantity)                 AS units_sold,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS gross_value
    FROM   order_items oi
    JOIN   orders   o ON o.order_id   = oi.order_id
    JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE  o.status <> 'CANCELLED'
    GROUP  BY p.category_id
)
SELECT b.root_name                        AS top_level_category,
       COUNT(*) - 1                       AS sub_categories,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.products_sold), 0)  AS products_sold,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.units_sold), 0)     AS units_sold,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.gross_value), 0)    AS gross_value,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COALESCE(SUM(s.gross_value), 0) DESC) AS revenue_rank
FROM   branch b
LEFT JOIN category_sales s ON s.category_id = b.category_id
GROUP  BY b.root_id, b.root_name
ORDER  BY revenue_rank

queries.title: R3 WITH RECURSIVE - referral chains from their original referrer
queries.description: R3. Recursive CTE: referral chains Business question: who started each referral chain, and how far did it spread (A referred B, B referred C, ...)?
queries.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE referral_chain AS (
    

    SELECT c.customer_id,
           c.full_name                       AS chain_start,
           0                                 AS depth,
           CAST(c.full_name AS CHAR(500))    AS chain
    FROM   customers c
    WHERE  c.referred_by IS NULL
      AND  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers x WHERE x.referred_by = c.customer_id)
